body_markdown:
Repairing cars has always been a mix of replacing and repairing parts. More often than not, the balance between the two shifts significantly depending on the age of your car. As cars get older, repair is more common, as the parts were built to be serviced and are also often unavailable. Modern cars, by comparison, are items designed for parts swapping. Does it have to be this way, though? What if we look at one common wear item that is popular to simply replace and see if it can be rebuilt at home? Let’s say, an alternator.


I recently had the alternator on my LS-swap 1985 Corvette fail. Intially I was annoyed it only lasted a year or so. I quickly got over that when I remembered how easy it is to swap out. A couple of clicks on the computer, a couple of days waiting for it to arrive, then drop the serpentine belt, remove one electrical connection and two bolts, swap the new one in, reverse the process, and[the whole swap](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/improve-your-classic-by-upgrading-your-alternator/) is done. Simple, easy, and the belt tension and alternator bolts are even the same 15mm-headed bolts. It seemed like the best-case scenario, until I saw a video about rebuilding a modern alternator from a motivated Australian.


I like to think of myself as pretty enterprising and willing to crack something open just to see what’s what, but opening up my alternator and having a peek didn’t even cross my mind. Of course, I wouldn’t have been as prepared as Jezza was when opening up the unit[pulled from under the hood](https://youtu.be/I6c1zf99wmk?si=nnfMToB7-Jok87lW) of a Holden pickup, but after seeing how relatively few things were going on inside, I think I might have to try next time.


Alternators work in a pretty simple way: The rotor and its magnets spin inside a housing filled with windings of copper wire. As the magnets spin past, they induce a current, transforming the mechanical energy of the turning engine into electrical energy now flowing into the battery and chassis wiring harness. With only one moving part, it is often the smaller electrical parts that fail. In the video, it was the slip rings that act as contacts to energize the magnets on the rotor. One broke, leaving the circuit open. A replacement was sourced—rather affordably, I might add—then soldered in, and the whole thing reassembled.


New slip rings solved the issues on this alternator and were an easy repair.


BushBound 4WD


Is it the most efficient means of repair? Probably not, and often alternators and generators are sold with a core charge, so most are sent back for professional rebuilding when we get “new” ones[to install](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/alternator-replacement-on-an-aging-daily-driver-again-part-i/) . The materials in these bits are not that intimidating when you get down to it. Maybe next time the alternator fails on one of my cars, I’ll at least give it a try. Would you?
